newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kuchma upbeat on IMF loan, U.S. relations.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma upbeat on IMF loan, U.S. relations.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma said on Thursday he was certain Ukraine would get a $2.5-$3 billion International Monetary Fund loan whose fate has been cast in doubt by a six-month delay in passing the budget.
Asked after a summit with the presidents of Romania and Moldova if the three-year Extended Fund Facility would be approved, Kuchma said: "I have no doubt in this."

The IMF has a mission in Kiev for talks until July 10 which could not be immediately reached. The IMF has said it may issue a smaller, interim stand-by deal while Ukraine meets about 10 conditions left from a wish -list of 41.

Kuchma also said he spoke to U.S. Vice President Albert Gore, who "confirmed the United States and Ukraine are strategic partners and that the U.S. administration would take this into account in its actions, including economic ones".

He added that a group of economic advisers would visit Ukraine on July 10-11 from the United States, whose desire to strengthen Ukrainian independence from Russia has put Kiev third in line after Israel and Egypt for U.S. cash.

Kuchma, who on Wednesday accepted the resignation of his prime minister Pavlo Lazarenko -- seen as a reform-shy politician with shadowy links to the energy sector -- said he would try to propose a new candidate before parliament broke up for summer in mid-July.

"The new prime minister must take action because what kind of reforms are they if they only make things worse," Kuchma said. "I will try to propose a new prime minister before parliamentary holidays."
Kuchma said he met leaders of eight parliamentary groups on Wednesday to discuss the issue of the next prime minister.
No clear candidate has emerged but Kuchma said it should not be a newcomer from the regions.

Kuchma has been under pressure for months from Western officials and Ukrainian reformers to sack Lazarenko, blamed in part for the slow passage of reforms and especially a very slow rate of privatisation.
